Chapter 10: Communication

Johns & Saks, Organizational Behaviour, 13th Ed. — Chapter 10 | Week 5 | Estimated study time: ~3–3.5 hours

Learning Objectives
  • Define communication and effective communication, trace the basic sender–receiver model, and explain why communication by the strict chain of command is often ineffective
  • Explain the factors that produce voice versus silence, including psychological safety and the mum effect
  • Explain the organizational grapevine, its main features, and how rumours differ from grapevine information
  • Review the role of verbal language (jargon, humour) and non-verbal language (body language, office décor, clothing) at work
  • Discuss Tannen’s gender differences in communication and how failing to recognize them causes problems
  • Discuss cross-cultural communication challenges (language, non-verbal behaviour, etiquette, social conventions, cultural context) and the strategies that deter miscommunication
  • Define computer-mediated communication and information richness, and match media to messages
  • Review personal strategies and organizational initiatives that improve communication

Section 1

Why This Chapter Matters

The chapter opens with a hospital, not a business. CRICO Strategies, the research arm of the company that insures Harvard-affiliated hospitals, examined 23,658 malpractice cases from 2009 to 2013. Communication failures were a factor in 30 percent of the cases, and over 7,000 involved failures — between medical staff, or between staff and patients — that harmed patients. The chapter reports that better communication might have avoided nearly 2,000 U.S. patient deaths (the cases include 1,744 deaths) and $1.7 billion in malpractice costs. In one case, a nurse failed to tell a surgeon that a patient had abdominal pain and falling red blood cell levels after an operation; the patient later died of a hemorrhage. In another, office staff took calls from a diabetic patient but never relayed them to the primary care provider, and the patient collapsed and died. The Joint Commission, which accredits healthcare organizations, estimates that miscommunication among staff while transferring patients contributed to 80 percent of serious medical errors.

Notice what kind of failure this is. Nobody lacked knowledge; the information simply did not reach the right person in a usable form. That is the textbook’s definition of ineffective communication, and it is why communication is an organizational behaviour topic and not just a skills topic: the report blamed heavy workloads, a hierarchical workplace culture, cumbersome electronic records, and constant interruptions — all features of the organization, not of any one person’s vocabulary. Boston Children’s Hospital attacked the problem with I-PASS, a structured method for shift handoffs that began in 2008. When nine other pediatric hospitals adopted it, medical errors dropped by 23 percent. The hospital’s safety advocates add the condition you will meet again in Section 3: programs like I-PASS only take off in a culture of psychological safety, where staff feel free to speak up without fear of being punished or ridiculed.

Memory Aid — I-PASS (the Chapter’s Own Mnemonic) Illness severity · Patient summary · Action list · Situation awareness and contingency planning · Synthesis by receiver. Direction rule: the first four letters are what the sender hands over; the last S is the receiver reading it back, which is exactly the feedback step in the communication model of Section 2. Trap: I-PASS is a fix for horizontal communication between shifts — the text says it works “without the up-and-down process” of the chain of command. Self-test: write the five items from memory, then say which one is feedback.

The rest of the chapter works outward from that story: the basic model and the formal chain of command (Section 2), the willingness to speak up (Section 3), the informal network that runs beside the chain (Section 4), the non-spoken messages in how we look and where we sit (Sections 5–6), the differences that cut across gender and culture (Sections 6–7), the digital media through which most messages now travel (Section 8), and what individuals and organizations can do about all of it (Section 9).

Where This Chapter Sits in Your Exam Plan Chapter 10 is taught in Week 5 (Oct 5–9) alongside Chapter 11. It is midterm material (Thursday, Oct 29), and it also falls inside the range of Group Assignment #2 (Weeks 5–9, Chapters 7–11; the in-class, closed-book written questions in the week of Nov 9–13). That overlap is a known trap: because the assignment range runs Chapters 7–11, it is tempting to file Chapter 10 under “assignment only.” It is not — Chapter 7 is final-exam material, while Chapter 10 and the first part of Chapter 11 are on the midterm track. Study for multiple choice first (names, lists, definitions), then rehearse the Name → Define → Apply → Recommend answer pattern on Practice Problem 5 for the assignment.
Start With Your Own Experience Dr. Kassaye opens the Week 5B lecture with a prompt: think of a time someone misunderstood something you said — perhaps your instructions seemed clear but the other person did something different. Why did it happen? Keep that episode in mind as you read: slide 3 asks “What helps or hinders sender-to-receiver communication?” and in the lecture the hindrances are unclear wording, distractions, assumptions, and unfamiliar terms or jargon. By Section 2 you will be able to say which step of the model your episode failed at.
Section 2

The Communication Model and the Chain of Command

The basic model (Learning Objective 10.1)

Communication is the process by which information is exchanged between a sender and a receiver. The simplest prototype is a one-on-one exchange. The sender must encode thoughts into some form that can be transmitted — words, tone, an email. The receiver must perceive the message and accurately decode it to reach understanding, and the receiver may then initiate feedback that tells the sender the message was received and understood. The model is valuable because it shows the many points where errors can occur, producing a lack of correspondence between what the sender meant and what the receiver understood. Encoding and decoding are especially error-prone when the message is inherently ambiguous or emotional: the textbook’s example is encoding a thought with a touch of humour and transmitting it by email, which can easily be decoded incorrectly (Figure 1).

Effective communication occurs when the right people receive the right information in a timely manner. Violating any one of those three conditions makes the episode ineffective — a correct message sent to the wrong person fails, a message that reaches the right person but is incomplete fails, and a correct, complete message that arrives after the decision was made fails. (The hospital cases above are all of these: the message existed but did not reach the right person, in full, in time.)

Vocabulary Trap — Encode vs. Decode The sender encodes; the receiver decodes. A scenario in which the speaker “chose confusing words” is an encoding problem; one in which the listener “took a polite phrase literally” is a decoding problem. The textbook’s Japanese–Norwegian example shows that the same breakdown can be blamed either way: the Norwegian client says the Japanese manager encoded unclearly, while the Japanese manager criticizes the Norwegian’s weak decoding. On the exam, read for who performed the faulty step.

Lecture Supplement — Week 5B: The Seven-Step Version of the Model

From Dr. Kassaye’s Week 5B slide 4 and recorded lecture. The textbook describes the same process in prose; the slide turns it into seven labelled steps, and group-assignment questions may ask you to walk through them.

The slide splits the model into a sender side and a receiver side: the sender thinks (decides what to communicate), encodes (puts the idea into words, symbols or gestures), and transmits (sends it through a channel such as email, telephone or conversation); the receiver perceives the message, decodes it (interprets it based on their own level of understanding), and reaches understanding (makes sense of it); then feedback goes back to the sender so that they can check whether the receiver understood what was intended. The textbook never labels “thinking” as a step, and it folds transmitting into the idea of a message that can be transmitted — but nothing in the lecture contradicts the text.

Memory Aid — “The Eager Teacher Prepares Daily Useful Feedback” Think · Encode · Transmit · Perceive · Decode · Understand · Feedback. Direction rule: the first three are the sender’s work, the next three are the receiver’s, and the last one runs back to the sender. Trap: perceiving is just receiving the message (reading or hearing it); decoding is interpreting it; understanding is the result. A receiver can perceive perfectly and still decode wrongly. Self-test: cover Figure 1 and label each of the seven as “sender” or “receiver.”
Worked Example — The Joke That Landed Flat
Dana, a team lead, emails her analysts: “Great — another ‘quick’ client call at 5 p.m. Friday. I’m thrilled.” She is joking about a client who always schedules late, and plans to take the call herself. One analyst, Omar, reads it as Dana being annoyed with the team and stays silent; the others assume the call is theirs.
IDENTIFY: a model-stage question - find the step that
  failed and who performed it.

APPLY (step by step):
  THINK        fine - Dana knows what she means.
  ENCODE       FAILS - she compresses sarcasm and humour
               into a few words. The textbook flags
               exactly this: humour sent by email is
               easily mis-encoded and mis-decoded.
  TRANSMIT     email is a lean medium: no tone of voice,
               no facial expression to signal "joking".
  PERCEIVE     fine - everyone reads the message.
  DECODE       FAILS - Omar reads it literally as
               irritation (and others miss that she will
               take the call).
  UNDERSTAND   the wrong meaning results.
  FEEDBACK     MISSING - nobody replies "are you joking?
               who is taking it?", so the error survives.

CONCLUDE: the error is spread across encoding, medium and
  missing feedback, not only Omar's decoding. Fix: state
  plainly who takes the call, save humour for a richer
  medium (or a face-to-face check-in), and invite a
  reply to confirm understanding.

Communication by strict chain of command (Learning Objective 10.1)

The lines on an organizational chart are lines of authority and formal reporting relationships — the chain of command. In theory, organizational communication could stick to this strict chain, and three necessary forms of communication could be accomplished along it.

DirectionWhat it isTextbook exampleLecture example (Week 5B)
DownwardFlows from the top of the organization toward the bottomA VP of retail banking tells regional managers to prepare a new mutual fund; they pass specifics to branch managers, who instruct financial advisorsA manager communicates instructions, policy, goals and performance feedback
UpwardFlows from the bottom toward the topA chemist conceives a new plastic formula and tells the R&D manager, who informs the relevant vice presidentEmployees send progress reports, concerns, feedback and suggestions to their manager
HorizontalOccurs between departments or functional units, usually to coordinate effort; in a strict chain it must go up to and then down from a common managerA salesperson’s customer idea must travel up through marketing and down through R&D to reach R&D staffSales coordinates with delivery to meet a customer need; colleagues share information, solve problems and avoid duplicated effort
Worked Example — Tracing a Message Through a University’s Chain of Command
Dr. Kassaye’s lecture shows a university’s structure: the provost and vice-presidents at the top, and in the academic line, deans reporting up, department heads reporting to deans, and faculty and staff reporting to department heads. A department head in one faculty wants to share a course with a department in a different faculty. Strictly following the chain, how does her request travel, and what can go wrong?
IDENTIFY: horizontal communication between two units in
  different faculties - so a strict chain must route it
  up to a common manager and back down.

APPLY: department head (A) -> her dean (up) -> a senior
  academic officer above both deans (up) -> the other
  dean (down) -> department head (B) (down). Four hops.
  - SLOWNESS: every hop waits on someone's inbox.
  - FILTERING: each person may summarize, water down or
    stop the message ("not a priority").
  - INFORMAL communication ignored: the two department
    heads could simply call each other.

CONCLUDE: the formal chain suits instructions and
  routine reporting, but for coordination the textbook's
  fixes are cross-functional teams, empowerment and
  direct links (Boston's I-PASS is the same idea).
  Note: reporting relationships vary from one
  organization to another, as the lecture stresses.

Deficiencies in the chain of command

A lot of organizational communication does follow the formal lines: directives pass downward, suggestions pass upward. But the formal chain is an incomplete and often ineffective path, for three reasons.

  • Informal communication is ignored. The chain fails to consider informal communication between members. Good ideas do not respect organizational boundaries, and informal networks (often supported by social media) can be important sources of innovation.
  • Slowness. Even when the chain transmits information faithfully, it can be painfully slow — especially for horizontal communication between departments, and it is a poor mechanism for reacting quickly to customer problems. Cross-functional teams and employee empowerment short-circuit the chain, as does Boston’s I-PASS.
  • Filtering is the tendency for a message to be watered down or stopped altogether at some point in transmission. Upward filtering often occurs because people are afraid management will use the information against them. Downward filtering is often due to time pressure or inattention to detail, but may be sinister: “information is power,” and a manager who fears an up-and-coming subordinate might filter crucial information to make the subordinate look bad at a staff meeting.

The textbook lists them in the order informal communication, slowness, filtering; the lecture slide (slide 5) lists informal communication, filtering, slowness. Same three items.

Memory Aid — “IFS” (Three Deficiencies) Informal communication ignored · Filtering · Slowness — “IF the chain is the only road, you get IFS.” Only three items, but the three are easy to confuse. Trap: a manager hoarding information to gain an edge is filtering (downward), not slowness; a message that is accurate but arrives late is slowness, not filtering. Self-test: for each of the three, give a one-sentence workplace example without looking back.
Exam Trap — Which Direction, Which Deficiency? Two separate questions get mixed up. Direction (downward, upward, horizontal) says where a message is going. Deficiency (informal communication ignored, filtering, slowness) says why the chain handles it badly. A salesperson’s idea travelling up and down to reach R&D is horizontal communication suffering from slowness. If the question describes a message being softened as it goes up, the direction is upward and the deficiency is filtering.
Section 3

Voice, Silence, and the Mum Effect

The free flow of information contributes to effective communication, and one aspect of that flow is employee voice: the constructive expression of disagreement or concern about work-unit or organizational practices (Learning Objective 10.2). Voice means “speaking up”; its opposite, silence, means withholding relevant information. Voice can be directed horizontally to teammates or vertically to the boss or upper management. When it is not morally or legally required, voice can be considered a form of organizational citizenship behaviour (Chapter 4) that lets organizations learn and change, so it is in their interest to encourage it. But speaking up is perceived as risky because of the power differentials built into organizations. Dr. Kassaye’s slide 8 groups the same three ideas — voice, psychological safety, and the mum effect — as what the “free flow of information” requires.

What promotes voice

More satisfied employees who identify more strongly with their work unit or organization are most likely to speak up, as are those who are conscientious and extraverted. Direct supervisors and higher-level managers play an absolutely critical role in creating a climate in which constructive dissent can emerge: both direct support (or lack of it) for dissent and the symbolic stories about what happened to those who spoke up are strong determinants of that climate. Meeting employees informally on their own turf and not unfairly punishing honest mistakes foster a positive climate. All of this contributes to psychological safety — the shared belief, described in Chapter 7, that it is safe to take social risks. High “voicers” also report less work stress than those who stay silent.

Memory Aid — “Satisfied Insiders Can Express” (Who Speaks Up) Satisfied · Identify strongly with the unit or organization (“insiders”) · Conscientious · Extraverted. Direction rule: all four push toward voice; the supervisor’s climate (support for dissent, stories about what happened to dissenters) can still override them. Trap: agreeableness and neuroticism are not on the textbook list. Self-test: name the four personal factors, then the two things a manager can do to build a safe climate.

What produces silence, and the mum effect

Self-censorship creates a climate of silence. One study found five implicit notions that contribute to it: I can’t attack the boss’s pet idea; I don’t have solid data to speak up; I can’t bypass the boss; I can’t publicly embarrass the boss; I can’t look like I’m not a team player. A more general factor is the mum effect: the tendency to avoid communicating unfavourable news to others. People would often rather “keep mum” than convey bad news that might provoke negative reactions. The sender need not actually be responsible for the bad news for the effect to occur, but it is even more likely when the sender is responsible — a nurse who mistakenly gives an incorrect drug dose may be very reluctant to tell the head nurse.

Memory Aid — “Polite Dogs Behave, Expecting Treats” (Five Reasons for Silence) Pet idea (can’t attack the boss’s) · Data (I don’t have solid data) · Bypass (can’t bypass the boss) · Embarrass (can’t publicly embarrass the boss) · Team player (can’t look like I’m not one). Note the end-of-chapter question asks for six reasons for silence: these five implicit notions plus the mum effect. Sorting rule: three of the five (pet idea, bypass, embarrass) are about not challenging or going around the boss; “data” is about the employee’s own evidence; “team player” is about the employee’s image with the group. Self-test: give all six, then one organizational fix for each (see the table below).

The mum effect is more pervasive than it first looks. Employees with strong aspirations for upward mobility are especially likely to hit communication difficulties with their bosses — they want to impress and so have strong motives to withhold bad news — whereas when managers are perceived as more open-minded, employees open up about negative events. The textbook’s organizational examples are blunt: a study of Nokia’s loss of the “smartphone battle” blamed middle managers’ reluctance to challenge top management’s overly optimistic view of the company’s technology, and the mum effect was implicated in management at Mitsubishi Materials failing to learn that quality-control data on flawed parts had been faked. And it does not run only upward: one study found that employees with good performance ratings were more likely to know them than employees with bad ratings, because managers avoided communicating bad news for which they were partly responsible. No wonder managers and employees often disagree about performance.

Reason for silenceWhat an organization could do (applying the text’s climate factors)
Can’t attack the boss’s pet ideaLeaders visibly invite challenge to their own proposals and reward those who offer it
No solid data to speak upMake clear that early concerns are welcome, not only fully proven ones
Can’t bypass the bossProvide protected routes (skip-level meetings, suggestion systems, hotlines — Section 9)
Can’t publicly embarrass the bossMeet employees informally on their own turf, where dissent is private and low-risk
Can’t look like I’m not a team playerFrame constructive dissent as part of the team’s job (voice as citizenship), and avoid punishing honest mistakes
Mum effect (reluctance to deliver bad news)Respond to bad news without punishing the messenger; managers model openness by sharing their own bad news downward
Vocabulary Trap — Voice vs. Silence vs. Mum Effect vs. Filtering Voice = constructive speaking up about disagreement or concern. Silence = withholding relevant information (the general behaviour). The mum effect = the specific tendency to avoid passing on unfavourable news, even when you are not responsible for it. Filtering = a message watered down or stopped in transmission through the chain (Section 2). A junior employee who spots a costly error and says nothing out of fear is showing silence driven by the mum effect; a supervisor who softens the same report on its way up is filtering. They overlap in practice, so look for the key word: bad news avoided → mum effect; message altered as it travels → filtering.

Lecture Supplement — Week 5B: Manager–Employee Communication

From Dr. Kassaye’s Week 5B slide 7 and recorded lecture. This list is not in the textbook chapter; it is examinable in the group assignments and is a natural written-answer topic.

Slide 7 says that effective manager–employee communication exists when the two sides agree and are sensitive about eight areas. In the lecture, the manager explains what employees must do and why, and both sides clarify priorities; employees should feel comfortable asking questions and raising concerns, because upward communication brings suggestions and feedback, and the manager’s leadership style should encourage listening and respectful dialogue.

  1. Job expectations: what, why, how, and with whom
  2. Time allocation: how employees should allocate their time
  3. Learning time: how long it should take to learn the job
  4. Pay: the importance employees attach to pay
  5. Authority: the amount of authority employees have
  6. Skills and abilities of employees
  7. Performance and obstacles: employee performance and obstacles to good performance
  8. Leadership style: the manager’s style
Memory Aid — “Every Team Leader Pays Attention to Skills, Performance, Style” Expectations · Time allocation · Learning time · Pay importance · Authority · Skills · Performance and obstacles · Style (leadership). Direction rule: the first five are about the job’s terms (what, time, learning curve, pay, authority); the last three are about the person and the manager (skills, performance, style). Trap: there are eight, and “pay” means how much employees care about pay, not their salary figure. Self-test: say all eight in order, then give one question a manager could ask to check agreement on each.
Link to Chapter 9 The chapter’s integrative question 2 asks how a manager’s leadership style affects manager–employee communication, using Chapter 9’s theories (ethical and authentic leadership, traits, behaviours, situational theories, participative leadership, LMX). Since Chapter 9 is also in Group Assignment #2’s range, expect questions that tie the two together: a participative or LMX high-quality relationship invites voice; an autocratic style invites silence.
Worked Example — Silence, the Mum Effect, and Filtering in One Product Launch
Priya, a junior developer, finds a bug that will delay a product launch by two weeks. She says nothing in the team meeting because her manager, Marcus, is up for promotion and she is hoping for a good review. A week later Marcus learns of the problem from a tester and tells the VP the launch has “minor timing risks.” The VP promises the client the original date.
IDENTIFY: three related failures - name each one and
  its direction.

APPLY:
  1) PRIYA: SILENCE, driven by the MUM EFFECT. She has
     unfavourable news and withholds it. The text adds
     that employees who want to impress their bosses
     have strong motives to withhold bad news.
  2) MARCUS: FILTERING (upward). He waters down "two-week
     delay" to "minor timing risks", likely out of fear
     the VP will use the news against him - the textbook's
     reason for upward filtering. Because he may feel
     partly responsible, the mum effect is also in play.
  3) THE CLIMATE behind both: weak PSYCHOLOGICAL SAFETY.
     Neither expects bad news to be received well.

CONCLUDE: the right people did not receive the right
  information in a timely manner (all three conditions of
  effective communication broken). Fix at the climate level:
  managers meet staff informally, do not punish honest
  mistakes, and respond to bad news constructively.
Further Reading
  • Wikipedia — Psychological safety — a short overview of the concept this section depends on (a shared belief that it is safe to take interpersonal risks); read it alongside the voice and silence material.
Section 4

The Grapevine

The chapter’s example comes from a steel mill where an author once worked: a sign at the gate read “X days without a major accident.” When it reset to zero, workers rarely took more than five minutes after entering to find someone who knew every detail. That information travelled through the grapevine (Learning Objective 10.3).

Characteristics of the grapevine

The grapevine is the informal communication network that exists in any organization, and it often cuts across the formal lines of communication recognized by management. We usually think of word of mouth, but emails and social media can transmit grapevine information too. Organizations often have several loosely coordinated grapevines — an administrative assistant in the “office grapevine” might pass something to a mail carrier, who passes it to the “warehouse grapevine” (Figure 3). The grapevine carries information relevant to organizational performance as well as personal gossip, and the two are often hard to tell apart (“You won’t believe who just got fired!”). One expert concludes that at least 75 percent of the non-controversial, organization-related information it carries is correct; personal and emotionally charged information is most likely to be distorted.

Who participates, and why

Personality may play a role: extraverts may be more likely than introverts to pass information on, and people lacking self-esteem may pass on information that gives them a personal advantage. Location matters too: occupants of high-traffic workstations (an air-conditioned computer room in a sweltering factory) get a steady stream of potential receivers, and jobs that require moving around the organization — IT troubleshooters are the textbook example — give their holders many chances to transmit. As for motives, the grapevine is a timely, inexpensive source of information not available through other channels; that information is an alternative source of power and influence open to everyone, not only those with access to formal channels; much of it involves releasing pent-up emotions about bosses or customers that cannot otherwise be expressed comfortably, and exchanging delicate information builds a bond of trust between sender and receiver; and some jobs are so boring that gossip supplies social and intellectual stimulation. In sum, some gossip can actually contribute to effective communication.

Memory Aid — Who Passes It On, and Why Transmitters (4): Extraverts · Low self-esteem · Location (high-traffic workstations) · Movement (jobs that roam the organization) — “Every Loose Lip Moves.” Motives (4): Information (timely, cheap) · Power (an alternative source) · Emotion (venting; trust bonds) · Boredom — “I Pass Every Bit.” Trap: physical location can matter more than personality for who hears the news first. Self-test: say both four-item lists, then give one example job for the “movement” item.

Pros and cons, and rumours

From the organization’s point of view the grapevine can keep employees informed about important matters such as job security — and in some organizations management is so lax at this that the grapevine is a regular substitute for formal communication. It can also test employee reactions to proposed changes without making formal commitments. It becomes a real problem when it becomes a constant pipeline for rumours. A rumour is an unverified belief in general circulation. The key word is “unverified”: a rumour can be true, but it is unlikely to remain true as it passes from person to person, since people cannot verify it and it is open to severe distortion. Rumours spread fastest and farthest when the information is ambiguous, when the content is important to those involved, when the rumour seems credible, and when the recipient is anxious. Tough competition, staff reductions, and restructuring have put a premium on rumour control, and the text’s advice is that organizations should avoid being “mum” about giving bad news (the mum effect again).

Memory Aid — “Always Investigate Crazy Announcements” (When Rumours Spread Fastest) Ambiguous information · Important to those involved · Credible-sounding · Anxious recipient. Direction rule: remove any one factor (clarify the facts, show the matter is routine, label it unverified, calm the audience) and the spread slows — and a manager’s fastest lever is usually clarity, which attacks ambiguity and anxiety at once. Trap: “the grapevine is always inaccurate” is false; mostly accurate on non-controversial organizational information, unreliable on personal and emotional content. Self-test: say the four conditions, then explain why a layoff rumour in a downsizing firm meets all four.
Vocabulary Trap — Grapevine vs. Rumour The grapevine is the network (the informal channel). A rumour is a kind of content that can travel on it: an unverified belief in general circulation. Most grapevine content is accurate; rumours, by definition, are unverified. A scenario about “the way news travelled between the office and warehouse” is the grapevine; one about “a story nobody could confirm that grew as it spread” is a rumour.

Lecture Supplement — Week 5B: A Third “Pro” and the Manager’s Role

From Dr. Kassaye’s Week 5B slide 9 and recorded lecture. The textbook gives two advantages of the grapevine (keeps employees informed; tests reactions to proposed changes). Slide 9 lists three pros — it adds “a potential informal recruiting source” (supported in the lecture by personal connections and networking) — and one con, the pipeline for rumours, incomplete information and misunderstanding. The lecture’s advice to managers is to recognize that the grapevine has value, listen to it to inform decisions, and keep providing timely, accurate updates through official channels.

Vocabulary Trap — Textbook vs. Lecture: Two Pros or Three? If a question asks for the advantages of the grapevine from the textbook, the answer is two: keeping employees informed and testing reactions to proposed changes. If it is built from the slides, three: add informal recruiting source. When an option lists “informal recruiting source” as a grapevine pro and nothing in the question points to the lecture, it is a lecture-only point — not wrong, but not in the book.
Worked Example — A Layoff Rumour on the Warehouse Floor
A distribution firm announces that it is “reviewing its network” after losing a major client. By Thursday the warehouse says a whole shift will be cut on Friday. The source is a driver who overheard a phone call; a supervisor repeats it as fact. Nothing official has been said, and workers are visibly anxious.
IDENTIFY: rumour on the grapevine. Check the four
  spread conditions.

APPLY:
  AMBIGUOUS  - "reviewing its network" tells nobody what
               will happen.
  IMPORTANT  - jobs are at stake.
  CREDIBLE   - a supervisor repeats it.
  ANXIOUS    - the audience fears job loss.
  All four conditions are met, so expect fast, wide
  spread - and distortion, since the claim is unverified.
  Transmitters: the driver (a roaming job) and the
  supervisor (a well-connected position).

CONCLUDE: do not try to "kill" the grapevine. Provide
  timely, accurate information through official channels
  (the lecture's advice), avoid being mum about bad news
  (the textbook's advice), and use a rich medium for an
  announcement this important (Section 8).
Section 5

The Verbal and Non-Verbal Language of Work

The verbal language of work (Learning Objective 10.4)

Jargon is specialized language used by job holders or members of particular occupations or organizations to communicate with one another. “OB” means organizational behaviour to management professors and obstetrics to physicians. Jargon is an efficient way to communicate with peers and gives a touch of status to those who have mastered it — the lecture adds that it lets people who share knowledge communicate quickly and precisely and strengthens a sense of professional belonging. But it is also a barrier: it can block clear communication between departments such as sales and engineering, and new members often find it intimidating and confusing (the lecture adds that newcomers may become reluctant to ask questions). It also separates insiders from outsiders: in the pharmaceutical industry “PC” can mean placebo control in R&D, personal computer in IT, politically correct in human resources, and preclinical in the regulatory division.

Humour is the textbook’s second verbal topic (it is not on the lecture slide). Humour works by affecting the emotions of the recipient: positive emotions facilitate attention, understanding and message acceptance, encourage creativity by making people less critical, act as an antidote to workplace stress, and — when leaders use self-deprecating humour — reduce social distance. The ambiguity of much humour also lets a communicator critique without arousing resentment (“face saving”), and leader humour facilitates trust, which stimulates feedback seeking by followers. Appropriate humour that is seen as funny raises a communicator’s status by making them seem competent and confident; but humour is risky: inappropriate jokes signal a lack of competence and reduce status, and aggressive humour is associated with follower norm violations and deviance. Managers should build a good relationship with subordinates before using humour so that the choice and timing are right.

The chapter’s Research Focus adds that small talk makes up about a third of adult verbal behaviour and is a double-edged sword. Methot and colleagues found daily workplace chit-chat was somewhat distracting but improved citizenship behaviour and well-being by day’s end. Rockmann and Pratt found off-site employees at a high-tech firm regretted losing office small talk and the work ideas that came with it, yet many chose to work off-site simply because others did — a vicious spiral in which people ended up in their less preferred location. Missing informal communication was often cited as a downside of working from home during the pandemic.

The non-verbal language of work

Non-verbal communication is the transmission of messages by some medium other than speech or writing. It often conveys “the real stuff” while words act as a smokescreen — the student who says “I understand” but somehow does not, the professor who says “come up any time” but does not mean it. (Verbatim minutes of a dramatic meeting read as boring precisely because the non-verbal cues are stripped out.) The two major forms are body language and the manipulation of objects — props, artifacts, and costumes (the lecture’s slide 11 uses the same two headings).

Body language

Body language is non-verbal communication by means of the sender’s bodily motions, facial expressions, or physical location in relation to the receiver. Two important messages it carries are how much the sender likes and is interested in the receiver, and the sender’s view of the relative status of the two. Senders communicate liking and interest by directing their torso toward the receiver, positioning themselves physically close, maintaining eye contact, and leaning forward. Senders who feel they have higher status than the receiver act more relaxed — casual placement of arms and legs, a reclining, non-erect posture, and a lack of fidgeting — and the greater the difference in relaxation between two people, the more they communicate a status differential. People can pose (look relaxed when they are not), but it is hard to regulate non-verbal behaviour under strong emotion, and observers can sometimes detect posing.

In employment interviews, where applicants are motivated to make a good verbal impression, interviewers may attend to non-verbal cues on the assumption that they are less censored. Smiling, gesturing, and eye contact have a favourable impact when they are not overdone, but body language is unlikely to overcome bad credentials or poor verbal performance — positive body language may give the edge to applicants who are otherwise equally qualified.

Memory Aid — “Truly Caring Employees Lean” (Signals of Liking and Interest) Torso toward the receiver · Closeness (physical proximity) · Eye contact · Lean forward. Sorting rule: engaged body language leans in (liking and interest); relaxed body language (casual limbs, reclining, no fidgeting) signals higher status. Trap: relaxation signals status, not liking — a reclining boss is not necessarily unfriendly, and a leaning-in subordinate is not necessarily lower in status by choice. Self-test: name the four liking cues, then the three relaxation cues.

Props, artifacts, and costumes

Office décor and arrangement communicate about the occupant. One study found students felt more welcome and comfortable in a professor’s office when it was tidy, decorated with posters and plants, and had the desk against the wall rather than between professor and student (a neat office signalled someone organized with time to talk; a personal touch signalled “I’m human”; no desk barrier meant no tangible barrier). Another study found strangers could accurately judge two Big Five traits from an office: neatness signals conscientiousness and distinctive décor signals openness to experience. Elsbach found that middle managers in California’s IT sector used décor to “profile” colleagues’ identity and status (Exhibit 10.1).

Office décorDistinctiveness inferencesStatus inferences
Family photosFamily oriented, balanced, not work focusedNot a “player”
Hobby photos, calendar, poster, artifactsAmbitious, outgoing, well-roundedUnprofessional
Funny, unusual artifacts and conversation piecesFun person, joker, offbeat, approachable, lazy, needs attentionNot serious, unprofessional
Formal décor, artifactsProfessional, successful, vain, distant, snobbishHigh status, authority figure
Informal, messy officeEasy-going, busy, true engineer, disorganized, unskilledUnprofessional
Awards, diplomasShow-off, hard-working, successful, pretentious, vainAccomplished, intimidating
Professional productsFunctional expert, “company person,” geekAccomplished
Ideological artifactsPatriotic, says “I have a social conscience,” extreme, radicalInsecure, unprofessional
Salient, flashy artifactsNeeds to get attention, flashyInsecure
High-conformity artifactsPredictable, reliable, conservative, not innovativeInsecure

Clothing also communicates. “Wardrobe engineer” John T. Molloy argues that clothing sends signals about competence, seriousness and promotability, because receivers unconsciously attach stereotyped meanings and treat the wearer accordingly; proper clothing will not make up for a lack of ambition or intelligence, but the wrong clothing can stop others from detecting those qualities. Speaking generally, conventionally well-dressed people communicate high status, competence and authority — which is why non-profits such as Dress for Success and Career Gear provide professional apparel to disadvantaged job seekers. Some successful people can “get away” with casual dress (Mark Zuckerberg’s hoodies), and research on the red sneakers effect shows non-conformity can signal status and competence, but only when it is seen as intentional and when it occurs in a prestigious context where conventional dress is expected (dressing down in the boardroom, not at the beach); the non-conformists were seen as more autonomous and in control. Clothing also affects the wearer: job applicants who dressed in formal interview gear felt they made a better impression and asked for a starting salary $4,000 higher than applicants in street clothes.

Vocabulary Trap — Non-Verbal vs. Body Language vs. Props/Artifacts/Costumes Non-verbal communication is the whole category: any message not carried by speech or writing. Body language is one form (bodily motion, facial expression, physical location); props, artifacts, and costumes is the other (office décor, arrangement, clothing). A scenario about posture, eye contact or leaning is body language; one about diplomas on a wall or a chair arrangement is an artifact; one about a lab coat or suit is a costume.

Lecture Supplement — Week 5B: Non-Verbal Examples and Context

From Dr. Kassaye’s Week 5B slide 11 and recorded lecture; useful as written-answer examples. The lecture illustrates the artifact category with four examples: a lab coat or gown identifies a researcher; formal dress can signal an official occasion; diplomas or qualifications on display signal expertise; and chairs around a shared table invite discussion between employer and employee. It stresses that such signals must be interpreted in context, because their meaning differs across cultures, individuals and situations — the same caution Sections 6 and 7 apply to gender and culture.

Worked Example — Two Offices, Two Messages
A first-year student needs to ask a professor for help. Dr. Alvarez’s office has a clean desk against the wall, two chairs angled toward each other, a plant, and a few posters. Dr. Brandt’s has a large desk between door and visitor, framed diplomas and awards on every wall, and a stack of papers. Which office is more likely to get the student to speak up, and what does the student infer about each professor?
IDENTIFY: office décor and arrangement are artifacts - a
  form of non-verbal communication (props, artifacts and
  costumes).

APPLY:
  ALVAREZ: matches the study the text cites - tidy,
    posters and plants, desk against the wall. The tidiness
    reads as organized and having time to talk; personal
    decoration reads as "I'm human"; no desk between the
    two parties means no tangible barrier. Likely inference:
    welcoming. The chairs echo the lecture's "chairs

    Elsbach's finding - "accomplished, intimidating" on

Section 6

Gender Differences in Communication

According to Deborah Tannen, there are gender differences in communication styles, and they originate in childhood (Learning Objective 10.5). Many girls see conversation as a way to develop networks of connection and intimacy; many boys see it as a way to achieve status and maintain independence; and these childhood differences persist in the workplace. A typical example: in a business meeting a woman comes up with a great idea but a male peer picks it up, spends more time talking about it, and gets the credit.

Tannen frames the differences as the “One Up, One Down” position. Men tend to be more sensitive to power dynamics and use communication to position themselves one-up. Women tend to be more concerned with rapport building and communicate in ways that avoid putting others down — so they often find themselves in a one-down position, which can hurt their careers. Tannen identifies nine key differences, and the lecture slide (slide 12) lists the same nine in the same order (Figure 4 and the table below).

#DifferenceMen tend to…Women tend to…How it goes wrong
1Getting creditBlow their own horn about good workDo so lessA man restates a woman’s idea and gets the credit
2Confidence and boastingBe more boastful about capabilities and minimize doubtsDownplay their certaintyMen are perceived as more confident
3Asking questionsAsk fewer (asking puts them one-down)Ask moreQuestions can read as one-down, so they are avoided
4ApologiesSee ritual apologies as weaknessSay “I’m sorry” as a rapport ritualRapport-building reads as weakness
5FeedbackBe blunt and straightforwardBuffer criticism with praise firstA man hears the praise, not the criticism, as the main message
6ComplimentsTake “what do you think?” literally and critiqueOffer a compliment (“Great presentation”)Each side answers a different question than the other asked
7Ritual oppositionAttack ideas, challenge in public, argue as a way to exchange ideasTake it as a personal attack to be avoidedDebate is felt as hostility
8Managing up and downSpend much more time with superiors, talking about achievementsBelieve good work alone gets recognizedWho you talk to influences who is recognized and promoted
9IndirectnessGive direct orders (expected of authority in North America)Give orders indirectly (“How would you feel about…?”)Seen as lacking demeanour and confidence

The key, according to Tannen, is to recognize that people have different linguistic styles and to be flexible enough to adjust when necessary: men should learn to admit when they make a mistake, and women should learn to be more direct when asking subordinates to do something. The styles women are accustomed to are most appropriate with other women, and likewise for men.

Memory Aid — “Self · Others · Power” (Nine Differences in Three Triples) The nine, in the textbook’s and the slide’s order, fall into three triples (this grouping is a study aid, not the textbook’s): SELF (how you present yourself) = Credit · Confidence · Questions (“CCQ”); OTHERS (what you say to and about others) = Apologies · Feedback · Compliments (“AFC”); POWER (how you handle disagreement and authority) = Ritual opposition · Managing up and down · Indirectness (“RMI”). Sorting rule from the chapter’s own summary: men tend to take credit, act confident, and express opposition; women tend to ask questions, apologize, and give compliments. Trap: the sorting is by tendency, and “asking questions” is the one where the stereotyped man (won’t ask for directions) asks fewer. Self-test: say CCQ, AFC, RMI and spell out each letter, then say which three of the nine the chapter summary assigns to men.
Vocabulary Trap — Feedback vs. Compliments, Ritual Opposition vs. Ritual Apology Feedback (difference 5) is about how criticism is delivered: women buffer it with praise, men are blunt. Compliments (6) is about how people respond when asked for their thoughts: women compliment, men critique. Ritual opposition (7) is the men’s habit of arguing as a way to exchange ideas; the ritual apology (4) is the women’s “I’m sorry” as rapport — one is attack-as-communication, the other is concern-as-communication. Mixing up the pairs is the most common wrong answer.

Lecture Supplement — Week 5B: Tendencies, Not Fixed Traits

From Dr. Kassaye’s Week 5B slide 12 and recorded lecture; the framing is the lecture’s, and it is the safe way to write about this topic in a group assignment. The lecture lists the same nine differences but frames them carefully: the differences are not fixed characteristics of men and women, and communication style varies between individuals. People face different expectations about how they should speak, express disagreement, or show leadership. Effective communication at work therefore requires you to recognize individual differences, clarify meaning, and evaluate contributions without gender stereotype classifications. The textbook’s own advice (be flexible, adjust your style) is consistent with this.

Link to Chapter 3 (Perception) The chapter’s integrative question 1 asks how perception shapes gender differences in communication, using Chapter 3’s system — the perceiver, the target person, and the situation. A listener decoding a woman’s buffered feedback or an indirect request, or a man’s blunt critique, uses their own style as the yardstick (perceiver), and misreading can then harden into gender stereotypes.
Worked Example — The Praise Sandwich Nobody Heard
After a client pitch, Sofia tells her colleague Ben: “You were great with the client — really warm. The pricing slide had a wrong number in it, which we can fix. Overall, a strong pitch.” Ben leaves pleased and does not correct the slide. Two weeks later the client questions the invoice. Sofia is frustrated; Ben says no one told him it was a problem.
IDENTIFY: Tannen difference #5, FEEDBACK (with a hint of
  #9 indirectness: "which we can fix" is a soft way to say
  "fix this").

APPLY: Sofia buffers criticism with praise to save face
  and avoid putting Ben in a one-down position - the
  women's tendency in the text. Ben, like the men the text
  describes, takes the praise as the main message. Both
  styles worked as intended; the mismatch caused the
  failure. In model terms: Sofia encoded the criticism so
  softly that Ben decoded it as optional.

CONCLUDE: per Tannen, both should adjust. Sofia can state
  the fix plainly ("please correct the pricing slide by
  Friday"); Ben can ask "is there anything I need to
  change?". Lecture caution: treat this as a style
  pattern, not a rule about men or women.
Section 7

Cross-Cultural Communication

The chapter opens this topic with an exchange between a Japanese businessman and his Norwegian client (Learning Objective 10.6). The Japanese manager wants to say he is uninterested in a sale, and, to be polite, says “That will be very difficult.” The Norwegian takes this to mean that unresolved problems remain, not that the deal is off, and asks how his company can help. The Japanese manager, believing he has said no, is mystified. From the Norwegian’s side the message was not encoded clearly; from the Japanese manager’s side, the Norwegian’s decoding was weak. The textbook examines five dimensions of cross-cultural communication.

Memory Aid — “Let Nobody Embarrass Strangers Carelessly” (Five Dimensions) Language differences · Non-verbal communication · Etiquette and politeness · Social conventions · Cultural context. The textbook’s order and the lecture’s slide 13 are identical. Direction rule: the first three are about how a message is expressed (words, body, politeness); the last two are broader habits and frames (conventions, context) — and cultural context is the organizing principle that explains many of the others. Trap: “cultural context” is a dimension, not a synonym for culture. Self-test: say the five, then give one textbook example for each.

1. Language differences

Communication is generally better between individuals or groups who share similar cultural values, and more so when they share a language — but sharing a language is no guarantee of perfect communication. A common language can lull visitors into complacency about real cultural differences: told “First class, mate” by a Qantas flight attendant when he reached for a magazine, an author laughed it off, but a visitor assuming “they speak English, they’re just like us” might attribute the brash informality to a rude personality instead of national style. Learning a second language helps, especially when it gives insight into the other culture’s style (the Japanese language has 16 subtle ways to say no). English has become the default language of global business, yet a study of over 800 foreign subsidiaries found that language differences between headquarters and subsidiaries pose substantial challenges: they fostered misunderstanding and conflict, parallel information networks, and a shift from face-to-face and telephone contact to less personal email. English-only policies (Nissan, Philips, Nokia, Siemens) are a common “solution,” but employees forced to speak English often feel reduced professional status and report extreme anxiety about communicating important business matters in a non-native language.

2. Non-verbal communication across cultures

Non-verbal communication does not necessarily travel better than words. Facial expressions: people decode basic emotions — anger, surprise, fear, sadness — well even across cultures (Americans, Japanese and Indigenous people in New Guinea read the same photos accurately), so watching the face often pays off; but collectivist cultures such as Japan tend to frown on displaying negative expressions. Gestures contribute to understanding within cultures but, except for literal mimicry (“I need food”), do not translate across them: the raised thumb is approval in the United States and an insult in Greece; the ring (“okay”) sign means okay to most English speakers but zero or worthless in parts of France; shaking the head means disagreement in English-speaking countries, while in Greece and southern Italy a head-toss does. Gaze: Latin Americans and Arabs favour an extended gaze, Europeans do not; in many parts of East Asia avoiding eye contact shows respect, while in North America it often connotes disrespect. Touch: people stand close and touch during conversation in Arab, Latin American and Southern European cultures, while Northern Europeans and North Americans keep their distance.

Memory Aid — “Foreign Guests Greet Tactfully” (Four Non-Verbal Channels) Facial expressions · Gestures · Gaze · Touch. Direction rule: faces travel best (basic emotions decode across cultures, with the collectivist caveat), gestures travel worst (symbolism is not shared). Trap: the thumbs-up example is an insult in Greece, and the ring sign means worthless in parts of France — do not swap the countries. Self-test: name the four channels and rank them from most to least transferable.

3. Etiquette and politeness

Cultures differ considerably in how etiquette and politeness are expressed, and very often it involves saying things one does not literally mean: a British executive who calls a proposal “interesting” might mean “it’s rubbish.” Literal decoding almost always leads to trouble. A North American manager who asks “Would you like to calculate those figures for me?” is giving a mild order, not an invitation to refuse — a foreign employee who has learned that Canadians speak directly may be unsure whether to say no. In some cultures politeness takes the form of modesty that seems excessive: a Chinese visitor, told his wife was very attractive, answered “No, no, my wife is ugly.” (A comparative study found American job applicants most likely to exaggerate their positive attributes, compared with Swiss and Icelandic applicants.) The Japanese use many set phrases, or “lubricant expressions,” to express sympathy, soften rejection, say no indirectly, or facilitate apology — the Japanese manager’s “that will be very difficult” was one. To Northern Europeans and North Americans these may seem like small talk or insincerity.

4. Social conventions

Beyond etiquette, several social conventions vary: directness (North Americans favour “getting down to brass tacks”; business meetings in the Arab world begin with a long period of informal chat, and Japanese negotiators can seem indirect and vague); greetings (“How are you?” in North America, which visitors may find hypocritical because no real answer is expected, versus “Where are you going?” elsewhere, which North Americans may find intrusive); loudness (people from “quieter” societies like the United Kingdom may view those from “louder” ones like the Middle East as pushy or intimidating); punctuality (expected and esteemed in North America and Japan, not viewed negatively in the Arab world and Latin America; one study found being on time connoted success in the United States and being late connoted success in Brazil); and personal information (North American professionals should not share too much personal information at work, so excessive personalization of an office with family or leisure photos is seen as less professional, as is discussing family life in a hiring interview — whereas in India such references can be appropriate). Exhibit 10.2 on the pace of life in six countries shows Japan as the most time conscious and Indonesia as quite leisurely, measured by clock accuracy, walking speed and post office speed.

Memory Aid — “Dogs Greet Loudly, Prefer Pats” (Five Social Conventions) Directness · Greetings · Loudness · Punctuality · Personal information. Trap: etiquette and politeness (what you say to be polite, often not literal) is a separate dimension from social conventions (directness, greetings, volume, time, personal disclosure) — a scenario about saying “interesting” for “rubbish” is etiquette, while one about arriving 20 minutes late is a social convention. Self-test: say the five, then give the textbook’s contrast (two cultures) for each.

5. Cultural context

Cultural context is the cultural information that surrounds a communication episode. Context is always important in decoding a message, but cultures differ in how much it influences meaning (Exhibit 10.3, Figure 5). In high-context cultures — many East Asian, Latin American, African and Arab cultures — the message is strongly influenced by the context in which it is sent, and literal interpretations are often incorrect (the Japanese manager really meant the deal was dead; the Chinese visitor did not really mean his wife was unattractive). In low-context cultures — North America, Australia, Northern Europe (excluding France) and Scandinavia — messages can be interpreted more literally, because more meaning resides in the message than in the context. Even “straight talk” is no straighter in meaning than high-context communication if one also learns to attend to context when decoding. The exhibit’s low-context end includes the Swiss, Germans, Scandinavians and North Americans.

The difference has implications in business negotiations. People from high-context cultures want to know about you and your company in great detail — the personal touch beats communicating through accountants and lawyers; they do not favour getting to the point quickly, preferring longer presentations and meetings that let people get to know one another (American negotiators who were more time impatient than Lebanese negotiators achieved lower negotiation outcomes); they give careful weight to the age and rank of the communicator, since age and seniority lend a message credibility (“younger fast trackers” do fine in low-context cultures where “it’s the message that counts”); and, because they devalue context, people from low-context cultures favour very detailed contracts, whereas high-context cultures place less emphasis on lengthy contracts because the context in which the deal is sealed is critical.

Memory Aid — “Kind Strangers Respect Customs” (Negotiating With a High-Context Culture) Know you (they want detail on you and your company) · Slow down (longer meetings, don’t rush to the point) · Rank matters (age and seniority of the communicator) · Contracts matter less (low-context cultures want detailed ones). Direction rule: each rule flips for a low-context partner — they want you to get to the point, the message to speak for itself, and the contract to be explicit. Self-test: say the four rules, then give the low-context opposite for each.
Vocabulary Trap — Textbook vs. Lecture: “Differences in Cultures” or “Within Cultures”? Slide 13 lists the three “important precautions” as Assume differences until you know otherwise; Recognize differences in cultures; Watch your language (and theirs). The textbook’s second precaution (in Section 10.8, “When in Rome…”) is “Recognize differences within cultures”: appreciating differences between cultures can blind you to differences among people inside a culture, which is what stereotypes do (your German employees have as many different personalities, skills and problems as your North American ones). The lecture slide appears to drop the word “within.” The textbook wording is the one that carries the meaning — and the one to use in written answers.
The Three Cross-Cultural Precautions (Slide 13 and Textbook Section 10.8) 1. Assume differences until you know otherwise. Caution says assume cross-cultural differences exist until proven wrong, because we project our own feelings onto ambiguous targets; be especially alert with proficient English speakers from cultures that emphasize harmony (e.g., Japan) — their good English tempts you to think they think like you, and their good manners stop them from telling you otherwise. 2. Recognize differences within cultures (above). 3. Watch your language (and theirs). Speak clearly, slowly and simply unless the person is very fluent; avoid clichés, jargon and slang (“I’m all ears,” “Let’s get rolling,” “So long”); and do not assume fluent speakers of your language are smarter, more skilled or more honest. The lecture adds practical steps: observe verbal and non-verbal signals, ask respectful questions to confirm understanding, clarify your expectations, and avoid assuming one gesture means the same thing for everyone.
Worked Example — Reading “That Will Be Very Difficult”
A Canadian sales manager presents a proposal to a prospective partner from a high-context culture. After a long first meeting spent mostly on the company’s history and family background, she asks for a decision. The partner’s representative smiles and says, “That will be very difficult.” She replies by offering a 10 percent discount and asks to schedule a signing. Why does the partner look uncomfortable?
IDENTIFY: dimension = ETIQUETTE AND POLITENESS, framed by
  CULTURAL CONTEXT (high- vs. low-context). Same pattern
  as the Japanese manager and Norwegian client.

APPLY:
  ENCODE: the partner uses a polite "lubricant expression"
    to say no without causing offence. In a high-context
    culture the meaning sits in the setting and
    relationship, not the literal words.
  DECODE: she decodes literally, as most low-context
    Canadians would - "difficult" = a problem to solve,
    so she tries to solve it with a discount.
  ALSO: the long opening meeting was not wasted time -
    high-context negotiators want to know you and your

  slow down, build the relationship, read context and
  tone, and ask a respectful, open question ("what
