  pushing a closing move.

The chapter’s Global Focus box shows the same dynamics at scale: French firm Naval Group, building submarines for Australia, found that lunch and meeting times caused friction (the sanctity of the French lunch break; a French “diplomatic 15 minutes” late versus Australian insistence that a one-hour meeting means one hour), and responded with a common-language effort, communication changes, and intercultural seminars and workshops for French staff.

Further Practice & Video
  • YouTube — Hand Gestures Around the World — the video on Week 5B slide 14; watch it to 1:48 as the slide directs and note which gestures change meaning across cultures.
  • Wikipedia — High-context and low-context cultures — the concept behind Exhibit 10.3; a quick reference for the contrast between explicit and implicit communication.
Section 8

Computer-Mediated Communication and Information Richness

Information richness (Learning Objective 10.7)

Does communicating digitally differ from communicating face to face? A good way to think about it is information richness: the potential information-carrying capacity of a communication medium. There are two dimensions: the degree to which information is synchronous between sender and receiver (two-way, in real time), and the extent to which both parties can receive non-verbal and para-verbal cues (e.g., tone of voice). A face-to-face conversation is very high in richness: the sender is present, audio and visual channels are synchronous, body language and verbal language both occur, and feedback is immediate and ongoing. A phone conversation is also fairly rich but limited to the audio channel — no body language. At the low end of synchronization, memos, letters and emails are essentially a series of one-way messages (though email, and especially texting, have clear potential for speedy response), and non-verbal and para-verbal cues are essentially absent in text-based media.

Vocabulary Trap — Non-Verbal vs. Paraverbal Cues Non-verbal cues are the visual signals: facial expression, eye contact, gestures, posture. Para-verbal cues travel with the voice but are not the words: tone of voice (the textbook’s example), and in the lecture, the pace or speed and volume of speech. A phone call has paraverbal cues but no non-verbal ones; a text message has neither; a video call has both. Do not confuse synchronization (timing, two-way and real-time) with cues (the signals carried): a text chat can be synchronous yet carry no cues.

Lecture Supplement — Week 5B: How the Lecture Defines Richness

From Dr. Kassaye’s Week 5B slide 15 and recorded lecture. The lecture covers richness only (slide 15); the media continuum, the strengths and weaknesses of CMC, and social media below are textbook-only. The lecture describes information richness as a medium’s ability to express meaning and support understanding, especially for complex, vague or ambiguous messages, and names the same two dimensions: the degree of synchronization (how participants exchange ideas and how quickly feedback comes; conversation allows immediate clarification, while email usually involves delay) and the degree of non-verbal and paraverbal cues. Slide 15 matches the textbook.

The media continuum

Exhibit 10.4 shows a continuum of communication media from face-to-face through digital media (Web 1.0: email, texting, video conferencing and chat-type decision support systems) to social media (Web 2.0: Facebook, LinkedIn, Twitter, YouTube and private company platforms). Web media are classified as computer-mediated communication (CMC) because they rely on digital technology to facilitate information exchange. They allow discussion and decision making without being in the same location, potentially saving time, money and travel. The distinguishing features of social media are that they let a large number of users simultaneously create, manipulate and distribute information, forming wide interactive networks that transcend formal organizational relationships — and that they are “socially transparent” (your communications are visible to co-workers) and sent without knowing exactly who might receive them or how they might be transformed.

FeatureFace-to-faceDigital media (Web 1.0)Social media (Web 2.0)
Physical access neededYes: same physical proximityNo: people need not be in the same locationNo
Number of people involvedLimitedBetween the two ends of the continuumCan foster large networks (maximum interdependence)
Synchronization and cuesHighly synchronous and loaded with verbal and non-verbal cues, so misunderstandings are easily sorted outVaries: email is less synchronous than chat or texting; text carries no non-verbal cuesText-based limitations apply, plus the special properties above
PermanenceNo permanent traceBetween the two endsIn principle permanent
AnonymityCannot be anonymousSome chat-type systems permit anonymous idea generationCan be sent anonymously

Strengths and weaknesses of CMC

Strengths. Chat-type group decision support systems that use text-based computer conferencing generate more ideas when brainstorming, in part because computer memory means people can “talk” at the same time. Some systems permit anonymous idea generation, so shy people may be less inhibited and anonymity can erase perceived or actual status differences: in one study of executives, men were five times more likely than women to offer an initial idea in a face-to-face meeting, but in an electronic meeting men and women were equally likely to do so. Weaknesses. When they meet for only a single session, computer-mediated groups making a decision take more time, make less effective decisions, and have less satisfied members than face-to-face groups — though over repeated sessions they gradually develop more trust and cooperation. Trust develops slowly in text-based CMC partly because people self-disclose less. The detachment of electronic communication can produce rude, impulsive messages and extreme views (flaming); informal modes of expression are prone to misinterpretation, especially sarcasm (hence emoticons); and a lack of non-verbal cues makes subtle trends toward decision consensus hard to spot. Email is even more prone to miscommunication than chat or texting because it is less synchronous: Kruger and colleagues found people strongly overestimate their skill at communicating and interpreting sarcasm, humour and emotion by email (people are egocentric and exaggerate how far others share their perspective), and some emails are read as more negative than intended.

Social media at work

Social media bring their own challenges on top of text-based limitations. Cyberloafing (updating your Facebook profile instead of serving customers; a large study found cyberloafers tended to be younger, extraverted, better-educated males, and that people with demanding jobs and those in organizations with policies against it did less of it); heavy social media consumption also reduces personal well-being. Cyberbullying — repeatedly directing negative messages at co-workers (Chapter 13) — is enabled by the capacity for anonymous mass communication. Social media also blur the work and non-work domains and senders may not know who receives their messages: employees have been fired for derogatory Facebook posts judged to have damaged the organization’s reputation, so many organizations have formal social media policies.

On the positive side, social media can aid knowledge sharing, collaboration and innovation and make employees feel connected and engaged because they facilitate voice. Security concerns have led many organizations to build private enterprise social media platforms accessible only to organizational members: they look and work like Facebook, can host blogs, wikis and document sharing, and let users message specific co-workers or broadcast widely. Workplace from Facebook is used by Canadian Tire, Columbia Sportswear and Save the Children; Telus runs TELUS Xchange, where, for example, an employee facing an unfamiliar custom-home installation can video the problem, narrate it and upload it, get solutions from colleagues across the country within ten minutes, and have the video tagged and archived for the next person. Research suggests the most important features of such platforms are chances to post, search, comment, and evaluate others’ ideas, and using them contributes to job performance and job satisfaction.

Memory Aid — “Computers Can Be Unkind” and “Pretty Smart Collaboration Engine” Social media challenges (4): Cyberloafing · Cyberbullying · Blurred work/non-work boundary · Unknown receivers — “Computers Can Be Unkind.” Enterprise social media features (4): Post · Search · Comment · Evaluate — “Pretty Smart Collaboration Engine.” Trap: cyberbullying is the challenge that distinguishes social media from less social digital vehicles such as email, because of the capacity for anonymous mass communication. Self-test: say both four-item lists, then say what makes enterprise platforms different from public ones (restricted to organizational members).
Rule of Thumb — Less Routine Messages Need Richer Media Reports and email are fine for recurrent, non-controversial, impersonal messages where information is merely being disseminated. Important decisions, intended changes, controversial messages, and emotional issues call for richer media (face-to-face, Skype, video). Text is often emotionally ambiguous, so watch for accidental conflicts that begin in text — and do not try to resolve a conflict by text. This rule is the single most examinable idea in Section 8.
Worked Example — Choosing a Medium for Three Messages
A manager must (a) tell the team that Friday’s stand-up is moving from 9:00 to 9:30, (b) announce a restructuring that eliminates two roles, and (c) sort out a disagreement between two analysts that began as a series of curt text messages. Choose a medium for each.
IDENTIFY: use the rule - less routine, more controversial
  or emotional messages need richer media.

APPLY:
  (a) Stand-up time: routine, non-controversial,
      impersonal information being disseminated.
      -> email or a team message is fine (lean medium,
      low synchronization, no cues needed).
  (b) Restructuring: an intended change with job
      consequences, hard to take, and emotional.
      -> richest available: face-to-face (or video if
      distributed), with a truthful, specific explanation
      and sincere tone (also Section 9).
  (c) Text-message conflict: text is emotionally
      ambiguous and not rich enough to resolve conflict.
      -> face-to-face (or at least a live call): synchronous
      feedback plus non-verbal and para-verbal cues let
      each side clear up misreadings immediately.

CONCLUDE: match the medium's richness to the message's
  routineness and emotional weight.
Further Reading
  • Wikipedia — Media richness theory — the theory behind the richness idea in this section; note it describes richness differently in places than Johns & Saks, so use it for background and the textbook for exam wording.
Section 9

Improving Communication: Personal and Organizational Approaches

People are learning that developing communication skills is as important as developing accounting or computer skills (Learning Objective 10.8). When you communicate well, people respond positively even if they are not happy with your message; poor communication can provoke a negative response that makes communication even worse, as the other party becomes resistant, defensive, deceptive or hostile. Figure 7 maps the toolkit: what you can do as an individual, and what an organization can build.

Personal approaches: basic principles of effective face-to-face communication

  • Take the time. Good communication takes time, especially for managers building rapport with employees. Not taking the time often leads to choosing the wrong medium: one of the authors saw a “don’t do this” memo sent to 130 employees because two had committed an offence — it irritated 128 people, and the two offenders did not grasp the problem. The boss should have met them face to face.
  • Be accepting of the other person as an individual with the right to feelings and perceptions that differ from yours; you can accept the person even if you are unhappy with something they did. Empathy (seeing things from their perspective) increases acceptance; acting superior or arrogant works against it.
  • Do not confuse the person with the problem. Be problem-oriented rather than person-oriented, and descriptive rather than evaluative: focus on what the person did, not who they are (“Don’t you care about the client’s needs?” imputes motives).
  • Say what you feel — practise congruence, a condition in which your words, thoughts, feelings and actions all contain the same message. Soft-pedalling bad news (saying someone’s job is probably secure when you think it is not) violates it, and so does failing to praise good work. Congruence is honesty or authenticity, not brutal frankness; and in some high-context cultures “saying what you feel” is done very indirectly, yet words and feelings are still congruent in their own context.
  • Listen actively. Good listening improves accuracy, shows acceptance, and encourages self-reflection in the speaker. Active listening is a technique for improving the accuracy of information reception by paying close attention to the sender, and it involves five techniques: watch your body language (sit up, lean forward, keep eye contact); paraphrase what the speaker means; show empathy; ask questions (have people repeat, clarify or elaborate; avoid leading questions); and wait out pauses instead of rushing to fill them.
  • Give timely and specific feedback. Do it soon and be explicit: speed maximizes the reinforcement potential of the message, and explicitness maximizes its usefulness to the recipient. Say what was good about the presentation to the client, and say it soon.
  • Tell a story. Stories are memorable, contextually rich, transmit information holistically and convey emotion; they can convey subtle knowledge, reinforce norms and values, stimulate change, tell a cautionary tale, or motivate action, with a “soft touch” compared with orders. Stories require a rich medium and are best told face to face.
Memory Aid — “Take A Pause: Speak, Listen, Feedback” (Six Principles) and “Be Patient: Empathize, Question, Wait” (Active Listening) Take the time · Accepting of the other person · Problem, not person · Say what you feel (congruence) · Listen actively · Feedback timely and specific — then add “tell a story” as the seventh. Active listening (5): Body language · Paraphrase · Empathy · Questions · Wait out pauses. Sorting rule: the first three principles are about your attitude (time, acceptance, focus), the next three about what you do (say, listen, give feedback). Trap: the text’s own summary list for 10.8 names “concentrating on the problem” and “telling stories” — same items, different wording. Self-test: say all seven principles, then the five listening techniques.
Vocabulary Trap — Congruence vs. Active Listening Congruence is about your own message being consistent: words, thoughts, feelings and actions all say the same thing (sender-side honesty). Active listening is about how you receive someone else’s message (receiver-side accuracy). A manager who says “your job is probably safe” while believing otherwise has failed congruence; a manager who nods but never paraphrases or asks questions has failed active listening. The two overlap only in that your body language while listening should also be congruent.

Personal approaches: “When in Rome…”

If you apply these principles carefully you are off to a good start in cross-cultural communication, but skills often deteriorate when people get nervous about a cross-cultural encounter. The textbook adds three precautions — assume differences until you know otherwise, recognize differences within cultures, and watch your language (and theirs). These are the same three covered in Section 7 and on lecture slide 13; the slide 16 list repeats them.

Organizational approaches

Employer branding promotes a clear and consistent image of the positive and distinctive features of an organization as an employer, so that effective communication begins before people join. It is used first to attract and recruit, but also to retain people by reinforcing commitment. It conveys tangible factors (pay, location, responsibilities, learning opportunities, start-up status, perks) and symbolic ones (prestige, innovation, informal culture, social responsibility), preferably through rich media: well-tailored websites, plus Facebook, Glassdoor and LinkedIn, and rankings such as Canada’s Top 100 Employers. Done correctly, branding gets the right information to the right people; inaccurate branding leads to poor hires and cynicism — as when Sephora, whose brand rests on a culture of caring and putting people first, had to confront the contradiction after a celebrity tweeted about being racially profiled in one of its stores.

Provision of explanations. Controversial policies (restructuring, layoffs, pay rollbacks, affirmative action) spark resistance, and, in line with the mum effect, many organizations announce them with little or no explanation, fearing to dwell on negative news or provoke lawsuits. That is a bad idea: explanations improve perceived fairness (the procedural and interactional fairness of Chapter 4). Two factors are critical: the adequacy of the explanation and the style of delivery. Adequate explanations are specific and detailed — the reasons for the policy, how the decision was made, and the benefits that will accrue — and the message should be truthful, sincere, respectful and sensitive, with sincere remorse and acknowledgment of suffering where appropriate, using a rich medium such as a personal appearance by the CEO. A research review found that an adequate explanation reduced employees’ tendency to retaliate by 43 percent, and that an inadequate explanation is seen as less fair than no explanation at all.

360-degree feedback (multisource feedback) is performance appraisal that uses the input of supervisors, employees (self), peers, subordinates, and clients or customers; Air Canada and Bell Canada use it. Appraisal has moved from purely downward communication to two-way and then multi-directional communication. It usually focuses on behavioural competencies rather than bottom-line performance, is usually used for development rather than salary determination, can produce contradictory feedback that ratees need help integrating, and leads to subsequent performance improvement.

Employee surveys and survey feedback. An employee survey is an anonymous questionnaire letting employees state candid opinions and attitudes, a useful means of upward communication; survey specialists must summarize (encode) results so that management can easily decode them, and periodic surveys let managers detect changes in feelings. When results are fed back to employees with management responses and plans for change, that survey feedback enhances downward communication and shows a commitment to two-way communication (Chapter 15 returns to surveys).

Suggestion systems are programs designed to enhance upward communication by soliciting ideas for improved work operations; they are a formal attempt to encourage useful ideas and prevent their filtering through the chain of command. A simple (electronic) suggestion box is usually ineffective because there is no incentive and no clear sign management has considered a submission. Better systems reward adopted suggestions (a flat fee of perhaps $500 for simple ones, or a percentage of anticipated savings for complex ones) and give feedback on each evaluation; strong publicity of adopted suggestions also enhances downward communication. One caution: paid systems can seem at odds with the free-flowing knowledge sharing that enterprise social media aim for, and can motivate secrecy rather than sharing.

Telephone hotlines and webcasts. Hotlines can use a news format (valuable in crises such as storms or strikes), serve as query systems (automated or a live Human Resources person), or let employees report unethical or illegal behaviour, anonymously; such hotlines are required by law for publicly traded U.S. firms, though many employees do not know about them or are reluctant to use them (Fox News noted there had been no hotline complaints about Bill O’Reilly before dismissing him for sexual harassment). Corporate webcasting is a rich, synchronous, interactive medium that can reach employees anywhere, with multiple presenters in several cities; good for general information, training and product introductions, with audience questions in writing, audio or video, and replay for those who missed it.

Memory Aid — “Better Employers Talk, Survey, Suggest, Inform, Mentor” (Organizational Approaches) Branding (employer) · Explanations (provision of) · Three-sixty (360-degree feedback) · Surveys (and survey feedback) · Suggestion systems · Inform (hotlines, webcasts, and the slides’ intranets) · Mentor (the slides’ “management training”). The first six are in the textbook; “intranets” and “management training” are lecture wording (see below). Sorting rule: surveys and suggestions go UP; branding, explanations and survey feedback go DOWN or OUT; 360-degree feedback and hotlines run both ways. Trap: “survey” is upward; “survey feedback” is the downward loop that closes it. Self-test: say the seven, then sort them into up, down/out and two-way.
Vocabulary Trap — Employee Survey vs. Survey Feedback, and Provision of Explanations vs. Employer Branding An employee survey collects opinions from employees (upward, anonymous); survey feedback tells employees what management heard and will do (downward). Employer branding communicates a consistent image of the organization as an employer to attract and retain (mostly outward, aimed at candidates and current staff); provision of explanations is how you justify a specific, usually controversial decision to those it affects. A question about publishing a recruitment image is branding; one about announcing layoffs with reasons is explanations.

Lecture Supplement — Week 5B: The Slide Lists Differ From the Textbook

From Dr. Kassaye’s Week 5B slides 16–17 and recorded lecture. The lecture slides present two lists with some differences. Slide 16, personal approaches (nine items): be accepting of the other person; do not confuse the person with the problem; say what you feel; listen actively; give timely and specific feedback; assume differences until you know otherwise; recognize differences in cultures; watch your language (and theirs); and take the time (listed last). The textbook lists “take the time” first and adds “tell a story,” which is not on the slide. In the recording, the lecture’s summary of this list stresses speaking clearly, taking time, accepting perspectives, expressing feelings clearly, listening with attention, asking questions to check understanding, timely and specific feedback, and noticing cultural and individual differences.

Slide 17, organizational approaches (seven items): employer branding; provision of explanations; 360-degree feedback; employee surveys and feedback; suggestion systems; intranets and webcasts; and management training. The textbook instead pairs telephone hotlines and webcasts and has no management-training item. In the recording the lecture also describes social media (LinkedIn, Facebook, WhatsApp) and websites as channels for sharing organizational performance and reaching employees across locations — the textbook treats social media (including enterprise social media, Section 8) as part of CMC, not as an item on the 10.8 list. The lecture defines management training as developing managers’ skills in listening, explaining, giving feedback, and handling difficult conversations.

Vocabulary Trap — Textbook vs. Lecture: Which List Is Which? Personal list: textbook = take the time (first), be accepting, concentrate on the problem, say what you feel, listen actively, timely and specific feedback, tell a story (+ three “When in Rome” precautions); slides = the same minus tell a story, with “take the time” last. Organizational list: textbook = branding, explanations, 360-degree feedback, surveys and survey feedback, suggestion systems, telephone hotlines and webcasts; slides = the same with intranets (instead of hotlines) and management training added. Most multiple-choice questions follow the textbook wording, so the textbook items are always safe; if an option names intranets or management training, check whether the question points to the lecture. In a written group-assignment answer, you can use items from either list.
Worked Example — Announcing a Pay Rollback
A manufacturer must cut all salaries by 5 percent for six months to avoid layoffs. HR proposes a one-paragraph email from the CEO: “Due to market conditions, salaries will be reduced by 5 percent effective next month.” Evaluate the plan and propose a better one.
IDENTIFY: a controversial policy - the provision of
  explanations applies, and the choice of medium matters
  (Section 8).

APPLY:
  - ADEQUACY: "market conditions" is not specific. The
    text asks for the reasons, how the decision was made,
    and the benefits (here: avoiding layoffs).
  - STYLE: the message must be truthful, sincere,
    respectful and sensitive, with sincere remorse and
    acknowledgment of suffering.
  - MEDIUM: controversial and emotional, so a rich medium -
    a personal appearance by the CEO (face to face or a
    live webcast with questions) - not a one-way email.
  - THE STAKES: an inadequate explanation is seen as LESS
    fair than none; an adequate one cut retaliation by 43%.
  - GRAPEVINE: a vague email invites rumours (ambiguous,
    important, anxious readers).

CONCLUDE: hold a CEO-led session, give specifics and the
  alternative (layoffs), express regret, take questions,
  and follow with written details and a survey so that
  employees' reactions come back up the chain.
Practice

Practice Problems

Problem 1 — Direction and Deficiency

A bank teller has an idea to shorten lineups. Following the formal reporting lines, she passes it to her branch manager, who decides it is “not worth bothering the regional office” and summarizes it to the regional manager as “some staff think queues are long.” Three weeks later a product team in a different division hears about it second-hand, after the idea has gone up to the VP of retail banking and down again. (a) Name each direction of communication involved. (b) Which chain-of-command deficiencies appear, and where? (c) Give one fix from the chapter.

Show answer
(a) The teller’s idea moves upward (teller → branch manager → regional manager → VP); because the product team is in a different division, getting it there is horizontal communication, which in a strict chain must go up to a common manager and then downward again. (b) Filtering: the branch manager watered down the idea (“some staff think queues are long”). Slowness: three weeks and several hops. Informal communication ignored: the teller and the product team never had a direct, informal channel, though good ideas do not respect organizational boundaries. (c) Any of: a suggestion system that lets employees send ideas upward without passing every level (designed to prevent filtering); a cross-functional team or empowerment to short-circuit the chain; or a direct, I-PASS-style structured handoff between units.
Problem 2 — Mum Effect, Silence, or Filtering?

A sales analyst notices that a forecast she prepared has a formula error that overstates next quarter’s revenue. She hopes to be promoted and tells nobody. Separately, her team lead learns of a second, unrelated problem from a customer; when he reports to his director he writes “minor customer concern” because he fears the director will hold it against him. Label each behaviour, say which is which, and explain how psychological safety could change the outcome.

Show answer
The analyst shows silence (withholding relevant information, the opposite of voice) driven by the mum effect — the tendency to avoid communicating unfavourable news. It is made stronger because she is partly responsible for the error and because people with upward-mobility aspirations have strong motives to withhold bad news. The team lead shows filtering: the message is watered down in transmission through the chain, and upward filtering often occurs because people fear management will use the information against them. (The mum effect is also present, since the news is bad — but the observable behaviour is a softened message, which is filtering.) Psychological safety — a shared belief that it is safe to take social risks — makes voice more likely: if managers meet employees informally, do not unfairly punish honest mistakes, and are seen as open-minded, the analyst is more likely to flag her error and the team lead to report the customer concern accurately.
Problem 3 — Richness and Medium Choice

(a) Name the two dimensions of information richness. (b) Place face-to-face conversation, a phone call, a text-message chat, and an emailed memo in order from richest to leanest, justifying the order with the two dimensions. (c) A manager wants to tell an employee that her role is being eliminated, and is considering email “to keep it factual.” Advise her.

Show answer
(a) The degree of synchronization (two-way, real-time) and the extent to which both parties receive non-verbal and para-verbal cues. (b) Face-to-face is richest: synchronous, with body language, tone and immediate feedback. The phone call is fairly rich: synchronous with para-verbal cues (tone of voice), but only the audio channel and no body language. The text-message chat can be speedy (potentially synchronous) but has no non-verbal or para-verbal cues. The emailed memo is leanest: essentially one-way and without cues. (c) Email is a poor choice: less routine, emotional and important messages call for richer media. She should deliver the news face to face (or video if she must), with a truthful, sincere, specific explanation. The email would also be prone to being misread as cold, since people tend to overestimate their ability to convey emotion in email, and an inadequate explanation is seen as less fair than none.
Problem 4 — A Gender-Difference Misread

In a meeting, Anika suggests a new onboarding checklist. Two minutes later her colleague David restates it more emphatically and is thanked for the idea. Afterwards Anika emails David: “Sorry to bother you — I might be wrong, but could we maybe look at the checklist together?” David replies to her draft with “Section 3 doesn’t work.” Anika, giving David feedback on his, writes, “Great energy! One tiny thing on slide 4 — otherwise fantastic.” David does not change slide 4. Identify the Tannen differences at work and explain what each person could do differently, with one caution about interpretation.

Show answer
Getting credit: David picks up Anika’s idea and spends more time on it, and gets the credit; Tannen’s “One Up, One Down” frame says men position themselves one-up while women avoid putting others down, leaving women one-down. Confidence/apologies/indirectness: “Sorry… I might be wrong… maybe” downplays certainty, uses a rapport-building apology, and makes a request indirectly, which can be perceived as lack of confidence. Feedback: David is blunt (“doesn’t work”); Anika buffers criticism with praise, so David hears the praise as the main message and ignores the criticism. What to do: following Tannen, recognize different linguistic styles and be flexible — Anika can state the request and the problem plainly (“please fix slide 4”) and claim credit for her idea in the meeting; David can admit his restatement came from her suggestion and ask what needs changing after praise. Caution (the lecture): these are tendencies, not fixed characteristics of men and women; individuals vary, so clarify meaning and evaluate contributions without stereotyping.
Problem 5 — Application: The Team That Never Raises Problems

Sam has just become operations manager at Northgate Logistics. Two weeks ago a warehouse software migration quietly failed. Sam first heard about it from a forklift driver in the cafeteria, and the details he heard were far worse than the weekly status email’s one-liner, “minor delays.” In one-on-one chats, staff say the last person who raised a problem was branded “negative,” and the senior team learned of the failure from a customer. Now a rumour that layoffs will follow is circulating. Sam plans to settle it with a short email. In the style of a group-assignment answer (Name → Define → Apply → Recommend), diagnose what is going wrong and recommend a package of changes, using at least five concepts from this chapter.

Show answer
Name & define: (1) Silence and the mum effect — silence is withholding relevant information; the mum effect is the tendency to avoid communicating unfavourable news. (2) Psychological safety — a shared belief that it is safe to take social risks; its absence is why voice (constructive expression of concern) is not happening. (3) Filtering — a message watered down or stopped in transmission. (4) Grapevine and rumour — the informal network, and an unverified belief in general circulation. (5) Information richness — a medium’s information-carrying capacity (synchronization plus non-verbal and para-verbal cues). (6) Effective communication — the right people receive the right information in a timely manner.

Apply: The failure is a textbook case of ineffective communication on all three conditions: the right people (senior team) did not receive the information, the content was distorted, and it was late. Staff behaviour shows silence driven by the mum effect: being labelled “negative” is the “symbolic story” that, per the text, shapes a climate in which no one feels safe to dissent — low psychological safety. The status email’s “minor delays” is upward filtering: bad news watered down, likely out of fear that management will use it against the sender. The grapevine worked as a channel (the news reached Sam through a forklift driver, with more accurate detail than the official email, consistent with its reliability on non-controversial organizational information) but the layoff rumour meets all four spread conditions — ambiguous, important, credible, and the audience is anxious. And Sam’s plan to use a short email is a poor medium choice: a controversial, emotional message needs a richer, synchronous medium.

Recommend: Personal: take the time to meet staff face to face; be accepting and focus on the problem, not the person, so that raising issues is not punished; listen actively (paraphrase, ask questions, wait out pauses); model congruence by sharing his own bad news honestly; give timely, specific feedback. Organizational: use a provision of explanations approach for the layoff rumour — an in-person (or live webcast) all-hands that is specific, truthful and sincere, since adequate explanations reduce retaliation by 43 percent while inadequate ones are seen as less fair than none; run an employee survey with survey feedback to rebuild upward communication and show it was heard; add a suggestion system or hotline for anonymous routes around the chain; and consider 360-degree feedback for managers. Together these target the climate (voice), the chain (filtering) and the medium (richness) at once.

Looking Ahead — Chapter 11: Decision Making This chapter was about getting the right information to the right people in time. Chapter 11 asks what they do with it: how people and groups make decisions, and where decision making goes wrong. The link is direct — filtered, late or missing information (the mum effect, filtering, silence) is one of the main reasons decisions go wrong, and group decision making depends on exactly the voice and psychological safety you studied here. Chapter 11 is also taught in Week 5; its first part is on the midterm track alongside Chapter 10, so study the two together.

  • Draw the sender–receiver model from memory, label the seven steps with “The Eager Teacher Prepares Daily Useful Feedback,” and say which step each of three scenarios failed at
  • Name the three directions of communication and the three chain-of-command deficiencies (“IFS”), and tell filtering from slowness
  • Distinguish voice, silence, the mum effect and filtering, and list the five reasons for silence (“Polite Dogs Behave, Expecting Treats”) plus the mum effect as the sixth
  • Say the eight areas of manager–employee communication from slide 7 (“Every Team Leader Pays Attention to Skills, Performance, Style”)
  • State the grapevine’s accuracy statistic, the four conditions for rumour spread, and the textbook vs. lecture lists of pros
  • Separate body language from props, artifacts and costumes; recall the four liking cues and the two conditions for the red sneakers effect
  • Recite Tannen’s nine differences (CCQ · AFC · RMI) and explain “One Up, One Down” without stereotyping
  • Name the five cross-cultural dimensions (“Let Nobody Embarrass Strangers Carelessly”), place cultures on the high- and low-context spectrum, and give the three precautions with the correct “within cultures” wording
  • Define information richness by its two dimensions, rank face-to-face, video, phone, text, email and memo, and apply the “less routine needs richer” rule
  • List the personal principles (“Take A Pause: Speak, Listen, Feedback”) and organizational approaches (“Better Employers Talk, Survey, Suggest, Inform, Mentor”), sorted by direction, and say where the lecture’s lists differ from the textbook’s
